extracted.intended_audience: researchers in mathematics education, cognitive psychologists, and philosophers of mathematics
extracted.subtask_description: Designing, conducting and interpreting empirical studies that assess how mathematicians appraise the aesthetic properties of proofs (including experimental manipulations, measurement scales, and statistical tests). Emphasis on hypothetico-deductive testing of causal hypotheses about aesthetic judgement and social influence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hypothetico-deductive (H–D) method
rubrics_metrics.description: From a hypothesis H deduce an outcome O, observe whether O occurs, and reason accordingly; H–D can function as a clincher or a voucher depending on results.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use H–D to derive risky predictions from theory. If ¬O is observed, use modus tollens to reject H (clincher mode). If O is observed, treat this as vouching (increasing plausibility rather than proving H). Be explicit about auxiliary assumptions and threats to internal validity that might invalidate the deduction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clinchers vs Vouchers / Popperian vs Hempelian reasoning
rubrics_metrics.description: Distinguish between tests that can decisively falsify (clinchers) and those that only vouch for hypotheses (vouchers); observing a predicted outcome does not deductively confirm H.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interpret negative results as stronger (potential falsification) than positive results (which only raise plausibility). Use replication and multiple successful predictions to increase confidence (vouching). Acknowledge philosophical caveats (e.g., Duhem thesis: auxiliary assumptions may be false).

rubrics_metrics.name: Power analysis and effect-size planning
rubrics_metrics.description: Determine sample size from a priori power analysis (example: required N=200 to have 80% power to detect d=0.4).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Perform power calculations for the anticipated effect size and desired power. Continue recruitment until target sample size is met or exceeded. Report the effect size used for planning and the achieved power where possible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Participant sampling and inclusion criteria
rubrics_metrics.description: Recruit participants representative of the target population (example: research-active mathematicians at UK/US universities); verify role (students vs faculty) and research area.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recruit via appropriate channels (e.g., departmental emails). Collect demographic/research-area data to enable controls and subgroup analyses. Ensure participants are active in the domain under study.

rubrics_metrics.name: Random assignment and minimal, well-defined manipulation
rubrics_metrics.description: Randomly assign participants to experimental conditions that differ only in the intended manipulation (example: ‘sourced’ vs ‘unsourced’ stimuli where the only difference is a single parenthetical citation).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Keep the stimulus identical across conditions except for the manipulation. Use lightweight manipulations where appropriate but consider whether manipulation strength and participant familiarity will permit detection of effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of short personality-style scale for proof appraisal
rubrics_metrics.description: Assess proof appraisals on four dimensions—aesthetics, intricacy, precision and utility—using four adjectives per dimension, each rated on a 5-point Likert scale; sum adjective scores to obtain dimension scores (range 4–20).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose adjectives to achieve acceptable internal reliability. Present adjectives in random order. Reverse-score items where appropriate (example: 'simple' reverse-scored for a dimension). Report how dimension scores are computed and their ranges.

rubrics_metrics.name: Include non-use (control) adjectives
rubrics_metrics.description: Include adjectives expected to receive low ratings (example: 'careless', 'crude', 'flimsy', 'shallow') to ensure some items function as negative controls.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use non-use adjectives to detect response biases or inattentive responding and to anchor the scale.

rubrics_metrics.name: Handling missing data and exclusion rules
rubrics_metrics.description: Define thresholds for participant exclusion and imputation (example: participants missing >5 of 20 adjective responses were deleted; up to 5 missing imputed using item means).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pre-specify deletion/imputation thresholds. Use appropriate imputation (e.g., item-mean) for small amounts of missing data and report numbers excluded and imputed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Randomized presentation order to avoid order effects
rubrics_metrics.description: Present adjectives (or other items) in a random order to each participant.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Randomization helps avoid systematic order effects that could bias ratings. Report randomization procedure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Measurement scale specification (Likert anchors & scoring)
rubrics_metrics.description: Use clearly labelled response options (example: very inaccurate, moderately inaccurate, neither, moderately accurate, very accurate) and define scoring conventions including reverse scoring.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Report exact anchor labels, scoring scheme, and any reverse-coded items so others can replicate scoring and interpretation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Collect and control for moderators (research area, role)
rubrics_metrics.description: Collect variables that may moderate response (example: pure vs applied mathematicians; student vs faculty) and include them in analysis (e.g., as ANOVA factors).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use prior literature to identify likely moderators. Collapse categories only where justified (example: applied mathematicians and statisticians collapsed due to small N). Report rationale for collapsing and control strategy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Statistical analysis & reporting standards
rubrics_metrics.description: Use appropriate inferential tests (example: 2×2×2 between-subjects ANOVA, t-tests) and report F/t values, degrees of freedom, p-values, effect sizes (ηp2 or d), and confidence intervals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pre-specify primary outcome and analytic model. Report interaction effects and follow-up comparisons. Provide exact p-values and effect-size estimates with CIs to aid interpretation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interpretation caveats: auxiliary assumptions and alternative explanations
rubrics_metrics.description: Acknowledge that observed effects may be due to auxiliary assumptions or alternative causal factors rather than the hypothesised mechanism (Duhem-style concern).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Discuss possible alternative explanations and threats to internal validity; avoid overclaiming causal certainty even when null hypotheses are rejected. Use replication and converging evidence to strengthen theoretical claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: External validity considerations
rubrics_metrics.description: Be explicit about the generalizability of laboratory/artificial stimuli (example: visual proofs and forced binary decisions may lack external validity even if they vouch for theory in the lab).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Discuss how experimental context may limit applicability to real-world settings; justify use of artificial stimuli as tests of theory and consider follow-up studies with more naturalistic tasks to assess external validity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Manipulation effectiveness may depend on participant familiarity
rubrics_metrics.description: A manipulation that signals prestige or aesthetic authority (example: citing Proofs from THE BOOK) will be effective only to participants familiar with that cue (example: more effective for pure mathematicians than applied mathematicians).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess or consider participant familiarity with cultural/historical cues used in manipulations. If familiarity varies, interpret subgroup effects accordingly and consider stronger manipulations or checks of manipulation awareness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of prior qualitative/observational work to generate experimental hypotheses
rubrics_metrics.description: Use findings from interviews, case studies or surveys (example: reading strategies identified by Weber & Mejía-Ramos) to generate testable hypotheses for H–D experiments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat qualitative studies as hypothesis-generating; design experiments to test these hypotheses quantitatively (vouching or clinching modes).

rubrics_metrics.name: Reading-strategy taxonomy as explanatory variables
rubrics_metrics.description: Categorize proof-reading behaviours (example: appealing to authority, line-by-line reading, modular reading) as ways mathematicians obtain conviction and as possible explanatory variables for appraisal differences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Measure or control for reading strategy where relevant; consider how different reading strategies might influence aesthetic or epistemic judgements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ethical & procedural transparency
rubrics_metrics.description: Obtain consent, ask minimal demographic questions, thank participants, and provide contact details for queries.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow ethical norms for human-subjects research: informed consent, data handling transparency, and participant debriefing/contact information.

rubrics_metrics.name: Link empirical findings to philosophical/theoretical positions
rubrics_metrics.description: Connect empirical results to broader debates (example: aesthetic realism vs anti-realism; literal vs reductive accounts) and discuss pedagogical implications.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use empirical evidence to inform, nuance, or challenge theoretical positions; explicitly state implications for education, theory, and future research directions.
